input.quote: A. No Application Management Revenue shall be due for any Corio Customer subscriptions utilizing the initial 3000 Software User licenses granted herein, subject to a minimum limitation of 40 Authorized Software Users per Customer
input.rationale: The Agreement imposes no minimum purchase commitment, volume quota or take-or-pay obligation on Corio, so it meets the preferred position that fees are payable only for usage or ordered services. Exhibit B charges Corio a license fee, an annual MarketSite.net access fee and an annual maintenance fee for services actually received, plus a revenue share calculated as a percentage of Application Management Revenue Corio actually invoices (p0157), and implementation fees on a time-and-materials basis capped by the Statement of Work (p0161) - all consumption- or order-based rather than guaranteed spend. The only "minimum" (p0158) is a 40-user threshold that conditions a revenue-share waiver in Corio's favour; it does not obligate Corio to buy anything and is therefore not a commitment we would resist. Likewise the sole "shortfall" reference (p0059) is a reciprocal audit true-up - "the appropriate party shall promptly pay the amount of such shortfall or refund such overpayment" - which is precisely the true-up mechanic the playbook prefers over a penalty, and it runs both ways. Exhibit D's sales and marketing items are expressly "non-binding," and the initial-customers item (p0205) is only a commercially reasonable efforts undertaking, not a purchase or volume commitment. Two points noted but not flagged: maintenance is structured so that continuation is conditioned on Corio electing to keep paying ("provided that Corio continues to pay the annual Maintenance and Support fees," p0055), which preserves a practical exit rather than locking in five years of fees; and the five-year initial term has no termination-for-convenience right, but that is a term/termination issue outside this rule and would duplicate another rule's commercial term.
